content: Reduced blood flow to critical organs such as the brain, heart, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract in very preterm infants can result in acute dysfunction and may lead to permanent damage. Various interventions, including the use of inotropes, corticosteroids, and volume expansion, have been employed to provide cardiovascular support in this population. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of early volume expansion on morbidity and mortality in very preterm infants. Additionally, it aimed to identify the most effective type of volume expansion, if such an intervention proved beneficial. The search strategy involved a comprehensive review of databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to July 2008. Randomized trials involving preterm infants born at ≤32 weeks of gestation or weighing ≤1500 g were included. Volume expansion was defined as the administration of at least 10 ml/kg of fluid within the first 72 hours after birth. The interventions studied included normal saline, fresh frozen plasma, albumin, plasma substitutes, or blood, compared to either no treatment or alternative forms of volume expansion. Data analysis followed standard methods, utilizing relative risk (RR), risk difference (RD), and weighted mean difference (WMD). Meta-analyses were conducted using a fixed-effects model, and only studies reporting outcomes for at least 80% of enrolled infants were included. Eight studies were included in the review. Five studies compared volume expansion to no treatment, while two studies compared different types of volume expansion in hypotensive preterm infants. One study evaluated the effect of volume expansion on blood flow in normotensive preterm infants. Importantly, no study specifically enrolled infants based on low blood flow. Four studies, involving a total of 940 very preterm infants, compared volume expansion to no treatment and found no significant difference in mortality (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.88–1.40). The large NNNI 1996 study reported no significant differences in severe disability (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.52–1.23), cerebral palsy (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.48–1.20), or the combined outcome of death or severe disability (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.80–1.24). Although one small study (Beverley 1985) suggested a reduction in periventricular/intraventricular hemorrhage (P/IVH) with volume expansion, this finding was not corroborated by other studies. No significant differences were observed in grade 3–4 P/IVH or the combined outcome of death or grade 3–4 P/IVH. Additionally, the NNNI 1996 study found no significant difference in the incidence of hypotension. One study reported a decrease in necrotizing enterocolitis and an increase in sepsis in infants who received fresh frozen plasma compared to no treatment. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution. When comparing albumin to saline in hypotensive infants, one study (Lynch 2008) found a significant increase in mean blood pressure and a reduced incidence of treatment failure (persistent hypotension requiring dopamine). However, another study (So 1997) and the meta-analysis of these two studies found no significant difference in treatment failure (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.54–1.07) or other clinical outcomes. The authors concluded that there is no evidence from randomized trials to support the routine use of early volume expansion in very preterm infants without cardiovascular compromise. Furthermore, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether volume expansion benefits preterm infants with cardiovascular compromise or to identify the most effective type of volume expansion. The observed increase in blood pressure in hypotensive preterm infants receiving albumin compared to saline in one trial is of uncertain clinical significance, as no other significant benefits were identified in the meta-analyses.
